questions.explanation: Text 2 reports that long checklists led more people to quit because missed items felt like failures, which cuts against the claim that such lists motivate. It does not endorse Castellano (A), reject goals (C), or compare task sizes (D).

questions.passage: Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, which would harm most other small fish. A layer of mucus on the clownfish's skin protects it from the stings. In return for this safe home, the clownfish may help the anemone by chasing away fish that would eat it and by leaving behind scraps of food.
questions.stem: According to the text, what protects clownfish from the anemone's stings?
choices: The clownfish's ability to swim quickly away from the tentacles.
Scraps of food that the clownfish leaves behind.
Other fish that chase predators away from the anemone.
A layer of mucus on the clownfish's skin.
questions.explanation: The text states that 'a layer of mucus on the clownfish's skin protects it from the stings.' Food scraps (B) and chasing away fish (C) are ways the clownfish helps the anemone, and speed (A) is not mentioned.

questions.passage: Photographer Obiageli Sørensen spent three winters photographing the same frozen lake at dawn. She could have chosen a new location each morning, but she believed that returning to a single place would train her to see small differences: the shifting color of the ice, the patterns left by wind in the snow, the way fog lifted differently from one day to the next. The resulting series, she says, is less about the lake than about learning to pay attention.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: By photographing one place again and again, Sørensen aimed to sharpen her ability to notice subtle changes.
Sørensen prefers photographing winter scenes to photographing summer scenes.
Sørensen chose the lake because it was the most beautiful location she could find.
Sørensen's photographs document damage to the environment around a frozen lake.
questions.explanation: The text explains that Sørensen returned to one place to 'see small differences' and that the series is 'about learning to pay attention.' B and C invent reasons the text never gives, and D is not mentioned.

questions.passage: Psychologist Nadia Farouk hypothesizes that people's snacking habits depend partly on what is in view: they are more likely to snack on fruit when it is placed where they can easily see it.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Farouk's hypothesis?
choices: Most office workers said they preferred apples to bananas.
Office workers ate more fruit during weeks when a fruit bowl sat on a table by the entrance than during weeks when the same fruit was kept in a closed cupboard.
Office workers who ate fruit in the afternoon reported feeling more alert.
Fruit kept in a closed cupboard stayed fresh longer than fruit left in an open bowl.
questions.explanation: Only choice B compares how much fruit was eaten when it was visible versus hidden, which is exactly what the hypothesis predicts. A, C, and D concern preferences, alertness, and freshness, not visibility's effect on eating.

questions.passage:
Average Number of Harbor Seals Resting on Shore at Selby Cove

Tide level  Seals
High tide   8
Mid tide    21
Low tide    47

Harbor seals often come ashore to rest on rocks and sandbars. A student observing the seals at Selby Cove claims that they come ashore in the greatest numbers when the tide is lowest. As support, the student notes that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: an average of 21 seals rested on shore at mid tide.
an average of 8 seals rested on shore at high tide.
an average of 47 seals rested on shore at low tide, more than at either mid tide or high tide.
the number of seals resting on shore at mid tide was more than twice the number at high tide.
questions.explanation: The claim is that numbers peak at low tide, so the support must compare low tide with the other levels; choice C does. D compares mid and high tide only, and A and B each give a single number.

questions.passage: Film historian Idun Maalouf argues that the Pellham Cinema Club, a film society founded in a small town in 1952, succeeded mainly because it showed films that local residents could not see anywhere else, not because of the discussions it held after each screening.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Maalouf's argument?
choices: Attendance at the club fell sharply after a nearby theater began showing the same kinds of films, even though the club continued its post-screening discussions.
Many members of the club said they especially enjoyed the discussions held after screenings.
The club showed an average of three films per month during its first decade.
The club's founder had worked as a newspaper film critic before starting the club.
questions.explanation: If attendance dropped once the films were available elsewhere while the discussions continued, the films, not the discussions, were drawing people. B points toward the discussions, the opposite of Maalouf's view; C and D do not address why the club succeeded.

questions.passage: Parrotfish scrape algae off coral with their beak-like teeth, and in the process they bite off bits of coral rock. They grind the rock into fine particles and pass it out of their bodies as sand. On some tropical islands, a large share of the white sand on the beaches was produced in this way. A sharp decline in the number of parrotfish near such an island would therefore most likely mean that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the island's beaches would become whiter over time.
coral near the island would stop growing entirely.
other kinds of fish would begin producing sand instead.
less new sand would be supplied to the island's beaches.
questions.explanation: If parrotfish produce much of the beaches' sand, fewer parrotfish would mean less new sand. A reverses the effect, and B and C make claims the text gives no basis for.

questions.passage: Psychologist Tavita Ekdahl asked two groups of volunteers to learn the same list of words. One group studied in a quiet room; the other studied in the same room while a radio played. Both groups were then tested in the room with the radio turned off. The first group recalled more words. Ekdahl cautions, however, that this result alone cannot show that background noise interferes with learning, because ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: some volunteers in the second group may have enjoyed the music on the radio.
the list of words may have been too easy for either group to find challenging.
only the second group was tested under conditions different from those in which it had studied.
the quiet room may have been more comfortable than the rooms volunteers usually study in.
questions.explanation: The first group studied and was tested in silence, while the second studied with noise but was tested without it, so the difference in scores could come from that mismatch rather than from noise harming learning. B applies equally to both groups, D concerns a room both groups shared, and A does not explain the result.

questions.passage: Every morning before the school bus came, Lena fed the goats, filled their water ______ checked the fence for any gap where the smallest kid might squeeze through.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The sentence lists three actions (fed, filled, checked), so a comma and 'and' belong before the last one. No punctuation (A) runs two actions together, the comma after 'and' (C) is misplaced, and a semicolon (D) cannot separate items in a simple list.

questions.passage: The cuttlefish is a master of ______ it can change both the color and the texture of its skin in less than a second to blend in with rocks, sand, or seaweed.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses ('The cuttlefish is a master of disguise' and 'it can change...') need a semicolon between them. A comma alone (B) is a comma splice, no punctuation (C) is a run-on, and 'which' (D) produces an ungrammatical clause.

questions.passage: When a photographer wants to freeze the motion of a hummingbird's beating ______ she must use either a very fast shutter speed or a brief, bright burst of light from a flash.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: 'When... wings' is a dependent clause, so a comma joins it to the main clause 'she must use.' A semicolon (A) or colon (B) must follow an independent clause, and 'and' (C) leaves the 'when' clause without a main clause to attach to.

questions.passage: Of all the strategies that participants in psychologist Siosaia Fifita's study tried for breaking an unwanted ______ replacing it with a different action proved the most effective, and simply trying to resist it proved the least.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: Everything up to 'habit' is an introductory prepositional phrase, and a comma separates it from the main clause beginning 'replacing it... proved.' A semicolon (A) or colon (D) must follow an independent clause, and without punctuation (B) the reader runs 'habit replacing it' together.

questions.passage: The students in the after-school film club ______ their first short movie last spring, and in June they screened it in the auditorium for the entire school.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: 'Last spring' and the past-tense 'screened' place the action in the past, so 'made' is correct. The present and future forms do not fit.

questions.passage: Clinging to rocks or coral, a feather star feeds without chasing its prey. The long, feathery arms of this animal ______ tiny bits of food from the water as currents carry them past.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The subject is the plural 'arms,' not 'animal,' which is part of the phrase 'of this animal,' so the plural verb 'catch' is needed. The other choices are singular.

questions.passage: Weathered by eighty winters and patched with boards of every color, ______ still stands at the top of the hill, though no animals have lived in it for years.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: the Kaur family has kept the old barn, which
it is the old barn that
questions.explanation: The opening phrase describes something weathered and patched, the barn, so 'the Kaur family's old barn' must follow it directly. A makes the family 'weathered by eighty winters'; B puts a vague 'it' in the subject position; C leaves the sentence without a main verb for 'the Kaurs.'

questions.passage: Tomato plants need plenty of direct sunlight to produce ripe fruit. ______ the Nakamura family planted their tomatoes along the south side of the garden, where the plants receive sun for most of the day.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The family's choice of a sunny spot follows from the plants' need for sun, so 'For this reason' fits. 'However' signals contrast, 'Meanwhile' a simultaneous event, and the planting is not an example of the need.

questions.passage: A photographer can make a busy city street look empty by leaving the camera's shutter open for several minutes. People walking through the scene never stay in one place long enough to be recorded clearly. ______ they leave little or no trace in the final image, while the buildings, which do not move, appear sharp.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: Because people keep moving, they fail to register in the long exposure; the third sentence states that consequence, so 'As a result' fits. 'In contrast' and 'Nevertheless' signal opposition, and the sentence is not an example.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Mudskippers are fish that live in muddy coastal areas, such as mangrove swamps.
• They can spend much of their time out of water.
• They breathe partly through their skin and the lining of their mouths.
• They use their front fins to move across the mud.
• Some species can climb onto mangrove roots.
questions.stem: The student wants to explain how mudskippers are able to breathe out of water. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Mudskippers live in muddy coastal areas such as mangrove swamps.
Out of water, mudskippers breathe partly through their skin and the lining of their mouths.
Mudskippers use their front fins to move across the mud.
Some species of mudskipper can climb onto mangrove roots.
questions.explanation: Only choice B explains how mudskippers breathe, through their skin and mouth lining. A gives their habitat, and C and D describe how they move.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Wanjiru Holt is a photographer who makes portraits with instant film.
• Each instant photograph develops within minutes.
• Holt makes two prints of each sitter and gives one to the person she photographed.
• She says this practice turns a portrait into 'a gift rather than something taken.'
• Her exhibition Given included 120 portraits.
questions.stem: The student wants to explain why Holt gives away one print of each portrait. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Holt's exhibition Given included 120 portraits made with instant film.
Holt makes portraits with instant film, which develops within minutes.
For each portrait, Holt makes two instant prints of the person she is photographing.
Holt gives each sitter one of the prints because, she says, doing so turns the portrait into 'a gift rather than something taken.'
questions.explanation: The goal is a reason, and only choice D gives Holt's stated reason for giving away a print. C describes the practice without explaining it; A and B give facts about the exhibition and the film.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Psychologist Oren Castellví studied adults trying to start a daily reading habit.
• One group set a goal of reading for 30 minutes a day.
• Another group set a goal of reading just one page a day.
• Over two months, the one-page group read on 52 days, on average; the 30-minute group read on 31 days.
• Once they had started reading, members of the one-page group usually read far more than one page.
questions.stem: The student wants to explain how a smaller goal could lead to more reading overall. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Castellví studied adults who were trying to start a daily reading habit.
In Castellví's study, one group set a goal of reading 30 minutes a day, while another set a goal of reading one page a day.
Adults who aimed to read just one page a day read on more days than those who aimed for 30 minutes (52 versus 31), and once they started, they usually read far more than one page.
Over two months, adults with a one-page goal read on 52 days, on average, while those with a 30-minute goal read on 31 days.
questions.explanation: Explaining 'more reading overall' needs both parts: the small goal got people reading more often, and once started they read well beyond it. Choice C gives both. D is tempting but shows only more reading days, not how much was read; A and B describe the setup.

questions.stem:
7x − 9 = 5x + 13

What is the solution to the given equation?
questions.explanation: Subtract 5x from both sides: 2x − 9 = 13. Add 9 to both sides: 2x = 22. Divide both sides by 2: x = 11.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to 3x(2x − 5) + 4x?
questions.explanation: Distribute 3x: 3x(2x) − 3x(5) = 6x² − 15x. Then add 4x: 6x² − 15x + 4x = 6x² − 11x.

questions.stem: Rolling Hills Bike Shop charges a flat fee of $12 plus $4.50 per hour to rent a bike. The function C(h) = 4.5h + 12 gives the total cost, in dollars, to rent a bike for h hours. What is the total cost, in dollars, to rent a bike for 6 hours?
questions.explanation: Substitute h = 6: C(6) = 4.5(6) + 12 = 27 + 12 = 39 dollars.

questions.skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
questions.stem: A bike shop assembles 3 bikes every 4 hours. At this rate, how many hours will it take the shop to assemble 27 bikes?
questions.explanation: 27 bikes is 27 ÷ 3 = 9 groups of 3 bikes. Each group takes 4 hours, so the shop needs 9 × 4 = 36 hours.

questions.stem:
x = 3y
x + y = 24

What is the solution (x, y) to the given system of equations?
questions.explanation: Substitute 3y for x in the second equation: 3y + y = 24, so 4y = 24 and y = 6. Then x = 3(6) = 18, and the solution is (18, 6).

questions.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = 2x² − 3x + 1. What is the value of f(−2)?
Two lines intersect at a point. Two of the angles formed are vertical angles with measures (3x + 10)° and (5x − 30)°. What is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Vertical angles are congruent, so 3x + 10 = 5x − 30. Then 40 = 2x, and x = 20. (Each angle measures 3(20) + 10 = 70°.)

questions.stem: At a science fair, tickets cost $5 for adults and $3 for students. The equation 5a + 3s = 420 represents a day on which the fair collected $420 from the sale of a adult tickets and s student tickets. If 60 student tickets were sold that day, how many adult tickets were sold?
questions.explanation: Substitute s = 60: 5a + 3(60) = 420, so 5a + 180 = 420. Then 5a = 240, and a = 48.

questions.stem:
2x² + 5x − 12 = 0

What is the positive solution to the given equation?
questions.explanation: Factor: (2x − 3)(x + 4) = 0, so x = 3/2 or x = −4. The positive solution is 3/2, or 1.5.

questions.stem: A concert venue sold 750 tickets for its Friday show. The number of tickets sold for its Saturday show was 16% greater than the number sold for the Friday show. How many tickets were sold for the Saturday show?
questions.explanation: 16% of 750 is 0.16 × 750 = 120, so the Saturday show sold 750 + 120 = 870 tickets. (Equivalently, 1.16 × 750 = 870.)

questions.stem: Dana deposits the same amount into her savings account at the end of every month and makes no withdrawals. The table shows the balance B(x), in dollars, in the account x months after she opened it. If B is a linear function, which equation defines B?
The function R models the number of riders on a city bus route each weekday t years after 2020, where R(t) = 850(0.96)^t. Which of the following is the best interpretation of 0.96 in this context?
choices: Each year, the number of weekday riders is 96% less than it was the year before.
Each year, the number of weekday riders decreases by 4.
Each year, the number of weekday riders is 4% less than it was the year before.
Each year, the number of weekday riders decreases by 0.96.
questions.explanation: Each increase of 1 in t multiplies R by 0.96, so each year's number of riders is 96% of the previous year's. That is a decrease of 100% − 96% = 4% per year, not a decrease by a fixed number of riders.

questions.stem: A recycling bin is shaped like a right rectangular prism that is 4 feet long, 2.5 feet wide, and 3 feet tall. How many cubic feet of material are in the bin when it is filled to 80% of its volume?
questions.explanation: The bin's volume is 4 × 2.5 × 3 = 30 cubic feet. 80% of 30 is 0.8 × 30 = 24 cubic feet.

questions.stem: Members of a recycling drive have collected 380 pounds of paper so far. They plan to collect 45 pounds of paper each week from now on. What is the least number of whole weeks from now after which the total amount of paper collected will be at least 800 pounds?
questions.explanation: The total after w weeks is 380 + 45w pounds. Solve 380 + 45w ≥ 800: 45w ≥ 420, so w ≥ 420/45 ≈ 9.33. The least whole number of weeks is 10. (After 9 weeks the total is 785 pounds; after 10 weeks it is 830 pounds.)

questions.skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
questions.stem: What is the mean number of bikes repaired per day over the 20 days?
questions.explanation: The total number of bikes repaired is 1(2) + 2(4) + 3(7) + 4(5) + 5(2) = 2 + 8 + 21 + 20 + 10 = 61. Dividing by the 20 days gives 61/20 = 3.05.
questions.passage:
Bikes repaired    Number of days
1                 2
2                 4
3                 7
4                 5
5                 2

The table summarizes the number of bikes a bike shop repaired each day over 20 days.

questions.skill: Systems of equations in two variables
questions.stem:
y = x² + 2x + 7
y = −2x + 3

The given system of equations has exactly one solution (x, y). What is the value of y?
questions.explanation: Set the two expressions for y equal: x² + 2x + 7 = −2x + 3, so x² + 4x + 4 = 0, or (x + 2)² = 0. Thus x = −2, and y = −2(−2) + 3 = 7.

questions.stem:
4(3x − 5) = 2(ax + 7)

In the given equation, a is a constant. If the equation has no solution, what is the value of a?
questions.explanation: Distribute: 12x − 20 = 2ax + 14. Collect terms: (12 − 2a)x = 34. If 12 − 2a ≠ 0, then x = 34/(12 − 2a) is a solution. If 12 − 2a = 0, the equation becomes 0 = 34, which is false for every x. So the equation has no solution when 2a = 12, that is, when a = 6.

questions.stem:
3x² + bx + 12 = 0

In the given equation, b is a positive constant. If the equation has exactly one real solution, what is the value of b?
questions.explanation: A quadratic equation has exactly one real solution when its discriminant is 0: b² − 4(3)(12) = 0, so b² = 144. Since b is positive, b = 12.

questions.stem: If one of the late trips is selected at random, what is the probability that it was a trip on Route B?
questions.explanation: Only the late trips matter. There were 16 + 24 + 20 = 60 late trips, and 24 of them were on Route B. So the probability is 24/60 = 2/5.
questions.passage:
On time    Late
Route A    84         16
Route B    66         24
Route C    90         20

The table shows the numbers of on-time and late trips for three bus routes during one month.

questions.stem: The system of equations 3x − 5y = 8 and kx + 10y = 11, where k is a constant, has no solution. What is the value of k?
questions.explanation: A system of two linear equations has no solution when its lines are parallel and distinct. The first line is y = (3/5)x − 8/5 and the second is y = −(k/10)x + 11/10. Parallel lines need −k/10 = 3/5, so k = −6. With k = −6 the y-intercepts, −8/5 and 11/10, differ, so the lines never meet.

questions.stem:
g(x) = a(x − 3)² + 5

The function g is defined by the given equation, where a is a constant. If g(1) = 13, what is the value of g(6)?

x² + y² + 6x − 10y = 15

In the xy-plane, the graph of the given equation is a circle. What is the area of the circle?
questions.explanation: Complete the square: (x² + 6x + 9) + (y² − 10y + 25) = 15 + 9 + 25, so (x + 3)² + (y − 5)² = 49. The radius is 7, and the area is π(7)² = 49π.

questions.stem: In the xy-plane, a line with slope 2/3 passes through the point (−3, 4). What is the y-coordinate of the y-intercept of the line?
questions.explanation: Write the line as y = (2/3)x + b. Substituting the point (−3, 4): 4 = (2/3)(−3) + b = −2 + b, so b = 6.

questions.stem:
(x + 4)/3 = (2x − 1)/5

What is the solution to the given equation?
questions.explanation: Multiply both sides by 15: 5(x + 4) = 3(2x − 1), so 5x + 20 = 6x − 3. Subtract 5x from both sides and add 3 to both sides: x = 23.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to (3x − 2)² − (3x − 2)(x + 4)?
questions.explanation: Factor out the common factor (3x − 2): (3x − 2)[(3x − 2) − (x + 4)] = (3x − 2)(3x − 2 − x − 4) = (3x − 2)(2x − 6).

questions.stem: A ramp at a bike park is 13 feet long and rises from the ground to the top of a platform 5 feet high. The ramp, the ground, and the vertical side of the platform form a right triangle, with the ramp as the hypotenuse. What is the tangent of the angle the ramp makes with the ground?
questions.explanation: The horizontal leg is √(13² − 5²) = √144 = 12 feet. For the angle at the ground, the opposite side is the 5-foot rise and the adjacent side is the 12-foot horizontal leg, so the tangent of the angle is 5/12.

questions.stem: A concert hall sold 420 tickets for one performance. Floor tickets cost $30 each and balcony tickets cost $18 each, and ticket sales totaled $9,360. How many balcony tickets were sold?
questions.explanation: Let f be the number of floor tickets and b the number of balcony tickets: f + b = 420 and 30f + 18b = 9,360. Substituting f = 420 − b gives 30(420 − b) + 18b = 9,360, so 12,600 − 12b = 9,360. Then 12b = 3,240 and b = 270.

questions.stem: For a science fair project, a student grew bean plants under different amounts of light. A scatterplot of the data has a line of best fit given by y = 1.8x + 4.5, where x is the number of hours of light per day and y is the plant's height, in centimeters, after 3 weeks. According to the line of best fit, what is the predicted increase in height, in centimeters, for every 5 additional hours of light per day?
questions.explanation: The slope, 1.8, is the predicted increase in height for each additional hour of light per day. For 5 additional hours, the predicted increase is 5 × 1.8 = 9 centimeters.

questions.skill: Systems of equations in two variables
questions.stem:
y = x² − 4x − 1
y = x + 5

Which of the following is a solution (x, y) to the given system of equations?
questions.explanation: Set x² − 4x − 1 = x + 5, so x² − 5x − 6 = 0, which factors as (x − 6)(x + 1) = 0. The solutions have x = 6 or x = −1, giving (6, 11) and (−1, 4). Of the choices, only (−1, 4) is a solution.

questions.stem: A bike shop's weekly revenue comes from bike rentals at $45 each and tune-ups at $20 each. The inequality 45r + 20t ≥ 900 represents the shop's weekly revenue goal, where r is the number of rentals and t is the number of tune-ups. If the shop does 12 tune-ups this week, what is the least number of rentals it needs to meet its goal?
questions.explanation: Substitute t = 12: 45r + 240 ≥ 900, so 45r ≥ 660 and r ≥ 660/45 ≈ 14.67. The number of rentals must be a whole number, so the least number is 15. (With 14 rentals the revenue is 630 + 240 = 870 dollars, which is short of 900.)

questions.stem: A bus leaves the start of its route and travels at a constant speed toward the end of the route. The function d(t) = 42 − 0.7t gives the distance, in miles, between the bus and the end of the route t minutes after the bus leaves. How many minutes after leaving does the bus reach the end of the route?
questions.explanation: The bus reaches the end of the route when d(t) = 0: 42 − 0.7t = 0, so 0.7t = 42 and t = 42/0.7 = 60 minutes.

questions.stem: A savings account earns interest compounded annually, and no deposits or withdrawals are made after the first deposit. The balance, in dollars, t years after the first deposit is given by B(t) = 2000(1.05)^t. What is the balance, in dollars, after 2 years?

questions.skill: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error
questions.stem: A bus system has 4,000 regular riders. In a survey of 250 of these riders selected at random, 36% said they would use a proposed express route. The margin of error for this estimate is 6 percentage points. Based on the survey, which of the following is the most plausible range for the number of all 4,000 regular riders who would use the express route?
questions.explanation: The plausible range for the percentage of all riders is 36% ± 6%, or 30% to 42%. Applied to all 4,000 riders: 0.30 × 4,000 = 1,200 and 0.42 × 4,000 = 1,680.

questions.stem: In the xy-plane, line ℓ passes through the points (−2, 7) and (4, −5). Line p is perpendicular to line ℓ and passes through the point (6, 1). What is the x-coordinate of the x-intercept of line p?
questions.explanation: The slope of line ℓ is (−5 − 7)/(4 − (−2)) = −12/6 = −2, so line p has slope 1/2. Through (6, 1): y − 1 = (1/2)(x − 6). Setting y = 0 gives −1 = (1/2)(x − 6), so x − 6 = −2 and x = 4.

questions.stem:
(ax + 3)(2x − b) = 6x² − 9x − 15

The given equation is true for all values of x, where a and b are constants. What is the value of a + b?
questions.explanation: Expanding the left side gives 2ax² + (6 − ab)x − 3b. Matching coefficients: 2a = 6, so a = 3, and −3b = −15, so b = 5. (Check: 6 − ab = 6 − 15 = −9, which matches.) So a + b = 3 + 5 = 8.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, point D lies on side AB and point E lies on side AC so that segment DE is parallel to side BC. The length of AD is 6, the length of DB is 9, and the area of triangle ADE is 24. What is the area of quadrilateral DBCE?
questions.explanation: Because DE is parallel to BC, triangle ADE is similar to triangle ABC with scale factor AB/AD = (6 + 9)/6 = 5/2. Areas scale by the square of the scale factor, so the area of triangle ABC is 24 × (5/2)² = 24 × 25/4 = 150. The area of quadrilateral DBCE is 150 − 24 = 126.

questions.stem: A bike shop sets the price of a bike 40% above the shop's cost for the bike. During a sale, the bike is sold for 15% off that price, for $357. What was the shop's cost for the bike, in dollars?
questions.explanation: The price is 1.40c, where c is the cost, and the sale price is 0.85(1.40c) = 1.19c. Since 1.19c = 357, c = 357/1.19 = 300 dollars.

questions.stem: The system of equations ax + 4y = 18 and 3x + 2y = b, where a and b are constants, has infinitely many solutions (x, y). What is the value of a + b?
questions.explanation: The system has infinitely many solutions only when the two equations describe the same line, so one equation must be a multiple of the other. Comparing the y-coefficients, 4 = 2 × 2, so the first equation is 2 times the second. Then a = 2 × 3 = 6 and 18 = 2b, so b = 9. Therefore a + b = 6 + 9 = 15.

questions.stem:
(x − 2)² − 5(x − 2) + 6 = 0

What is the sum of the solutions to the given equation?
questions.explanation: Let u = x − 2. Then u² − 5u + 6 = 0, which factors as (u − 2)(u − 3) = 0, so u = 2 or u = 3. Then x − 2 = 2 or x − 2 = 3, giving x = 4 or x = 5. The sum of the solutions is 4 + 5 = 9.

questions.stem:
f(x) = x² − 6x + c

The function f is defined by the given equation, where c is a constant. The minimum value of f(x) is −4. What is the value of f(1)?
questions.explanation: Complete the square: f(x) = (x² − 6x + 9) + (c − 9) = (x − 3)² + (c − 9). The minimum value is c − 9, so c − 9 = −4 and c = 5. Then f(1) = 1² − 6(1) + 5 = 0.

questions.skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
questions.stem: At a recycling drive, 12 volunteers collected a mean of 45 pounds of cans each. Two of the volunteers were Ari and Bea, and Bea collected twice as many pounds of cans as Ari. The mean amount collected by the other 10 volunteers was 42 pounds. How many pounds of cans did Bea collect?
questions.explanation: All 12 volunteers collected 12 × 45 = 540 pounds, and the other 10 collected 10 × 42 = 420 pounds, so Ari and Bea together collected 540 − 420 = 120 pounds. If Ari collected a pounds, then a + 2a = 120, so a = 40, and Bea collected 2(40) = 80 pounds.

questions.stem: A bike shop earns a profit of $80 on each city bike and $120 on each mountain bike it sells. This week the shop can sell at most 25 bikes in total, and it wants a total profit of at least $2,400 from these sales. What is the greatest number of city bikes the shop can sell this week and still meet both conditions?
questions.explanation: Let c be the number of city bikes and m the number of mountain bikes: c + m ≤ 25 and 80c + 120m ≥ 2,400. For a given c, profit is greatest when m is as large as possible, m = 25 − c. Then 80c + 120(25 − c) ≥ 2,400 gives 3,000 − 40c ≥ 2,400, so 40c ≤ 600 and c ≤ 15. Selling 15 city bikes and 10 mountain bikes earns exactly 1,200 + 1,200 = 2,400 dollars, so the greatest number is 15.

questions.stem:
(x + 1)/(x − 2) = 12/(x² − 4)

Which of the following gives all the solutions to the given equation?
questions.explanation: Since x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2), multiply both sides by (x − 2)(x + 2), where x ≠ 2 and x ≠ −2: (x + 1)(x + 2) = 12. Then x² + 3x + 2 = 12, so x² + 3x − 10 = 0, or (x + 5)(x − 2) = 0. The value x = 2 makes a denominator 0, so it is not a solution. The only solution is x = −5.

questions.stem:
x² + y² − 4x + 2y = 20

In the xy-plane, the graph of the given equation is a circle. The circle passes through the point (5, k), where k > 0. What is the value of k?
questions.explanation: Complete the square: (x − 2)² + (y + 1)² = 20 + 4 + 1 = 25. Substitute x = 5 and y = k: 9 + (k + 1)² = 25, so (k + 1)² = 16 and k + 1 = 4 or k + 1 = −4. Then k = 3 or k = −5. Since k > 0, k = 3.

questions.stem:
x/3 + 5 = 12

What is the solution to the given equation?
questions.explanation: Subtract 5 from both sides: x/3 = 7. Multiply both sides by 3: x = 21.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to 4(x² − 3x) − 2(x² + 5)?
questions.explanation: Distribute: 4x² − 12x − 2x² − 10. Combine like terms: 2x² − 12x − 10.

questions.skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
questions.stem: At a concert attended by 1,200 people, 3 out of every 8 people bought a T-shirt. How many of the people at the concert bought a T-shirt?
questions.explanation: 3 out of every 8 people is 3/8 of the people: (3/8)(1,200) = 450.

questions.stem: A rider's bus fare card has a balance of $40. Each ride costs $2.50, so the balance, in dollars, after n rides is given by f(n) = 40 − 2.5n. What is the balance, in dollars, after 6 rides?
questions.explanation: Substitute n = 6: f(6) = 40 − 2.5(6) = 40 − 15 = 25 dollars.

questions.stem:
(x − 3)(x + 8) = 0

What is the positive solution to the given equation?
questions.explanation: A product is 0 only when one of its factors is 0: x − 3 = 0 or x + 8 = 0, so x = 3 or x = −8. The positive solution is 3.

questions.stem: A storage box at a bike shop is shaped like a cube with edges 3 feet long. What is the volume of the box, in cubic feet?
questions.explanation: The volume of a cube is s³: 3³ = 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubic feet.

questions.stem:
2x + y = 20
y = 3x

If (x, y) is the solution to the given system of equations, what is the value of y?
questions.explanation: Substitute 3x for y in the first equation: 2x + 3x = 20, so 5x = 20 and x = 4. Then y = 3(4) = 12.

questions.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = 3(2)^x. What is the value of f(4)?

questions.skill: One-variable data: distributions and measures of center and spread
questions.stem:
72, 85, 91, 68, 79, 88

The list gives the scores that 6 projects received at a science fair. What is the range of the scores?
questions.explanation: The range is the greatest value minus the least value: 91 − 68 = 23.

questions.stem: In the xy-plane, a line passes through the points (0, 3) and (4, 11). Which equation represents the line?
questions.explanation: The slope is (11 − 3)/(4 − 0) = 8/4 = 2, and the line crosses the y-axis at (0, 3), so its y-intercept is 3. The equation is y = 2x + 3.

questions.skill: Systems of equations in two variables
questions.stem:
y = x² − 4x
y = 12

If (x, y) is a solution to the given system of equations and x > 0, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Substitute 12 for y: x² − 4x = 12, so x² − 4x − 12 = 0, which factors as (x − 6)(x + 2) = 0. So x = 6 or x = −2, and since x > 0, x = 6.

questions.stem: The balance in a savings account decreased from $1,250 to $1,000 after a withdrawal. By what percent did the balance decrease?
questions.explanation: The decrease is 1,250 − 1,000 = 250 dollars. As a percent of the original balance, 250/1,250 = 0.2, or 20%.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, AB = AC, and the measure of angle A is 40°. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle B?
questions.explanation: Because AB = AC, the angles opposite those sides, angle C and angle B, are congruent. Then 40 + 2B = 180, so 2B = 140 and B = 70°.

questions.stem:
7 − 2x ≤ 3x − 8

Which of the following is the solution to the given inequality?
questions.explanation: Add 2x to both sides: 7 ≤ 5x − 8. Add 8 to both sides: 15 ≤ 5x. Divide both sides by 5: 3 ≤ x, that is, x ≥ 3.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to 4x² − 25?
questions.explanation: 4x² − 25 is a difference of two squares, (2x)² − 5², so it factors as (2x − 5)(2x + 5).

questions.stem: What is the value of g(5)?
questions.explanation: The slope is (6 − (−4))/(2 − 0) = 10/2 = 5, and g(0) = −4 is the y-intercept, so g(x) = 5x − 4. Then g(5) = 5(5) − 4 = 21.

x    g(x)
0    −4
2    6

The table gives two values of the linear function g.

questions.stem: In right triangle ABC, angle C is the right angle, AB = 20, and sin A = 0.6. What is the length of BC?
questions.explanation: sin A = (side opposite angle A)/(hypotenuse) = BC/AB. So BC/20 = 0.6, and BC = 0.6 × 20 = 12.

questions.stem: On Saturday, a bike shop sold 25 items, each of which was either a helmet or a bike lock. Helmets cost $30 each and bike locks cost $18 each, and the shop collected $606 from these sales. Which system of equations can be used to find h, the number of helmets sold, and b, the number of bike locks sold?
questions.explanation: The shop sold 25 items in all, so h + b = 25. Helmets brought in 30h dollars and locks 18b dollars, so 30h + 18b = 606. (Solving gives 13 helmets and 12 locks.)

questions.stem: The value of a used bike, in dollars, t years after it is bought is modeled by V(t) = 600(0.85)^t. According to the model, what is the value of the bike, in dollars, 2 years after it is bought?
In the xy-plane, a line passes through the points (1, 2) and (k, 8), where k is a constant. The line is parallel to the graph of y = 3x − 5. What is the value of k?
questions.explanation: Parallel lines have equal slopes, so (8 − 2)/(k − 1) = 3. Then 6 = 3(k − 1), so k − 1 = 2 and k = 3.

questions.stem: A jar at a science fair contains only red marbles and blue marbles. If one marble is selected at random, the probability that it is red is 2/5. After 12 blue marbles are added to the jar, the probability that a randomly selected marble is red is 1/4. How many marbles were in the jar before the blue marbles were added?
questions.explanation: Let n be the original number of marbles, so 2n/5 of them are red. After 12 blue marbles are added, (2n/5)/(n + 12) = 1/4, so 4(2n/5) = n + 12, or 8n/5 = n + 12. Then 3n/5 = 12 and n = 20. (The jar had 8 red and 12 blue marbles; afterward 8 of the 32 marbles are red.)

questions.stem:
x² + kx + 12 = 0

In the given equation, k is a constant. One solution to the equation is 3. What is the other solution?
questions.explanation: Substitute x = 3: 9 + 3k + 12 = 0, so 3k = −21 and k = −7. The equation is x² − 7x + 12 = 0, which factors as (x − 3)(x − 4) = 0. The other solution is 4. (The product of the solutions is 12, and 12/3 = 4.)

questions.passage: Seed banks store samples of crop varieties in cold, dry vaults so that the varieties can be recovered if they disappear from farmers' fields. Because stored seeds slowly lose their ability to sprout, staff must ______ test the samples, checking each batch on a regular schedule and replacing any that no longer germinate.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Checking each batch 'on a regular schedule' is testing routinely. 'Rarely' contradicts the regular schedule, and 'reluctantly' and 'accidentally' describe attitudes or chance, which the text does not suggest.

questions.passage: When engineer Tomás Arriaga designed a footbridge for a remote mountain village, he chose a simple rope-and-plank structure instead of steel. The materials could be carried up narrow trails by hand, and villagers could repair the bridge themselves with tools they already owned. For a place so hard to reach, this ______ design was a sensible choice.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The bridge is a 'simple rope-and-plank structure' that villagers can repair themselves, so its design is uncomplicated. 'Elaborate' and 'costly' contradict that description, and nothing in the text says the bridge was meant to be temporary.

questions.passage: In many communities, recipes for festival dishes are passed down by example rather than written down. Anthropologist Keziah Mwangi found that such recipes are rarely ______: each cook adjusts the spices, the cooking time, or the proportions to suit the household, so that no two families in a village prepare the dish in exactly the same way.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The colon introduces constant variation from cook to cook, so the recipes are rarely fixed. 'Shared' is tempting, but the recipes are passed down through families, so they are shared; what the colon describes is variation.

questions.passage: Early windmills had sails that the miller had to turn into the wind by hand. Later designs added a small fan mounted at right angles to the main sails, which rotated the mill's cap automatically whenever the wind shifted. Historian Rhoda Farrant argues that this device, though easy to overlook, was hardly ______: it freed millers from constant watching and allowed mills to run safely through the night.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: 'Though easy to overlook' and the benefits listed after the colon show that the fan was important, that is, hardly incidental. 'Hardly indispensable' and 'hardly automatic' contradict the text, and 'hardly original' does not fit, since the colon explains the fan's importance, not whether it was new.

questions.passage: Farmers who plant the same crop in a field year after year often find that yields decline, because the plants draw down particular nutrients and pests that feed on that crop build up in the soil. Rotating crops, or planting a different crop in the field each season, can interrupt both problems. A legume such as clover, for example, adds nitrogen to the soil, and pests adapted to the previous crop find little to eat.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that farmers should stop growing legumes such as clover.
To describe the history of a traditional farming technique.
To explain how a farming practice addresses problems caused by planting the same crop repeatedly.
To compare the yields of several different crops.
questions.explanation: The text names two problems of planting one crop repeatedly and explains how rotation solves both, using clover as an example. It gives no history (B), makes no yield comparison (D), and presents legumes favorably rather than arguing against them (A).

questions.passage:
The following text is from a story. Nadia is traveling by train to visit her grandmother.

For the first hour Nadia kept her guidebook open on her knees, checking each station name against the map and marking it with a small pencil tick. The towns went by in the order the book promised. Somewhere after the river, though, the ticks stopped. When the conductor came through to announce the last stop, the book was lying closed on the seat beside her, and Nadia was leaning against the window, watching the hills slide by.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It shows a character's attention shifting from carefully tracking the journey to absorption in the passing scenery.
It describes a problem with a train schedule and how a character solves it.
It contrasts a character's feelings about her grandmother with her feelings about the train.
It presents a character's memories of an earlier trip along the same route.
questions.explanation: Nadia begins by ticking off each station in her guidebook, then the ticks stop, and at the end the book is closed while she watches the hills. There is no schedule problem (B), and the text never describes her feelings about her grandmother (C) or an earlier trip (D).

questions.passage: Engineers designing a water pump for small farms first built a version with lightweight alloys and a precisely machined impeller. In laboratory trials it outperformed every existing model. In the field, however, it broke down within weeks: grit in the irrigation water wore away the finely tuned parts, and no local workshop could make replacements. The team's second design used heavier, cheaper parts that any blacksmith could forge. It was less efficient on paper but ran for years.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It explains why the first design performed well in laboratory trials.
It suggests that laboratory trials are generally a poor guide to how any machine will perform.
It describes the conditions under which the second design was tested.
It presents a failure that accounts for the different priorities of the design described next.
questions.explanation: The third sentence shows the first pump failing because its parts wore out and could not be replaced, which explains why the second design favors sturdy, locally made parts. Choice B overgeneralizes: the text describes one machine, not laboratory trials in general.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Many agricultural scientists have promoted planting a single high-yielding rice variety across large areas, arguing that it produces more food per hectare than the mix of traditional varieties farmers once grew. Agronomist Paulo Esteves points to regional harvest records showing that total output rose sharply after farmers adopted such varieties.

Text 2
Yield in an ordinary year is only part of the picture. When a disease or pest adapted to a particular variety arrives, a field planted entirely with that variety can lose most of its harvest at once, while a field of mixed varieties usually loses only the susceptible share. Measured across both good years and bad, a mixed planting may prove the more dependable source of food.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Esteves's argument in Text 1?
choices: By disputing the accuracy of the harvest records that Esteves cites.
By suggesting that his evidence may not account for the losses a single variety can suffer when a disease or pest strikes.
By agreeing that planting a single variety is always the better choice for farmers.
By arguing that traditional varieties produce more food per hectare in ordinary years.
questions.explanation: Text 2 accepts high yields in ordinary years ('only part of the picture') but warns that a single variety can lose most of its harvest to one disease or pest, a risk Esteves's output figures may not capture. Choice D contradicts that concession, and Text 2 never questions the records themselves (A).

questions.passage: For centuries, farmers in the high Andes have preserved potatoes by making chuño. During the dry season, when nights are freezing and days are sunny, they spread potatoes on the ground outdoors. The potatoes freeze at night and thaw during the day, and people press out the released water by walking on them. The result is a light, dry potato that can be stored for years, providing food in seasons when fresh crops are scarce.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Andean farmers use the region's freezing nights and sunny days to turn potatoes into a food that keeps for a long time.
Potatoes grow better in the high Andes than in any other region.
Chuño is more nutritious than fresh potatoes.
Andean farmers plant potatoes only during the dry season.
questions.explanation: The text describes how the freeze-and-thaw process produces a potato 'that can be stored for years.' Choice D confuses when potatoes are preserved (the dry season) with when they are planted; B and C are not discussed.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a story. Ruben has just arrived in a coastal town where he does not speak the language.

Ruben had practiced the phrase for ordering coffee all through the ferry crossing, but when the woman behind the counter looked up at him, it vanished. He pointed at the cup on the next table instead. She nodded, filled a cup, and then, without being asked, set a small almond pastry beside it and waved away his coins. By the time he reached the harbor wall, he had decided to come back the next morning and try the phrase again, properly this time.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ruben regrets traveling to a town where he cannot speak the language.
Ruben is disappointed that the café does not serve the drink he wanted.
Ruben learns that the townspeople would rather visitors not attempt their language.
Although Ruben's attempt to speak the local language fails, a stranger's kindness leaves him eager to try again.
questions.explanation: Ruben forgets his phrase, but the woman's unasked-for generosity sends him off determined to return and 'try the phrase again.' Choice A ignores that hopeful ending; B and C are contradicted, since he gets his coffee and nothing suggests the townspeople discourage him.

questions.passage: Plant biologist Hana Obuya hypothesizes that tomato plants grown near basil suffer less insect damage than tomato plants grown alone because the strong scent of basil makes it harder for insect pests to locate the tomato plants.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Obuya's hypothesis?
choices: Tomato plants grown near basil were taller, on average, than tomato plants grown alone.
In a greenhouse trial, tomato pests located tomato plants less often when the surrounding air carried basil scent than when it did not.
Basil plants grown near tomatoes produced more leaves than basil plants grown alone.
Many gardeners report that they enjoy growing tomatoes and basil together.
questions.explanation: The hypothesis says basil's scent keeps pests from finding tomatoes, and choice B shows exactly that effect. Choice A concerns plant height, not insects; C and D say nothing about pests.

questions.passage:
Average Yield of Three Wheat Varieties at Kestrel Valley Trial Farm (tons per hectare)

Variety      Full irrigation  Reduced irrigation
Amberline    6.2              3.1
Dovecrest    5.4              4.6
Marrowfield  5.9              3.8

Researchers grew three wheat varieties with full and with reduced irrigation to find the best choice for farmers facing water shortages. They concluded that Dovecrest was the most promising variety for such farmers, noting that although ______
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the text?
choices: Amberline produced 6.2 tons per hectare under full irrigation, Marrowfield produced 5.9 tons per hectare.
Dovecrest produced the highest yield under full irrigation, it lost more than any other variety when water was reduced.
Dovecrest had the lowest yield of the three varieties under full irrigation, it had the highest yield under reduced irrigation.
all three varieties yielded less under reduced irrigation, Amberline's yield fell by half.
questions.explanation: Farmers facing shortages need the best yield with less water; choice C concedes Dovecrest's lowest full-irrigation yield (5.4) and then gives its highest reduced-irrigation yield (4.6). Choice B misreads the table, and A and D never mention Dovecrest.

questions.passage: Anthropologist Teodora Lisboa argues that the communal bread ovens once found in many villages of a mountainous region did more than save fuel. Because families baked on assigned days and waited together while their loaves baked, she contends, the ovens also served as places where news was exchanged and disputes were settled.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lisboa's argument?
choices: Village records often describe agreements between feuding families as having been reached 'at the oven,' and older residents recall baking days as the time they learned of births, deaths, and engagements.
Communal ovens used much less wood per loaf than the small ovens that individual households later installed.
The ovens were built of local stone and could hold dozens of loaves at once.
Baking days were assigned by a village official, who changed the schedule each year so that no family always had the least convenient day.
questions.explanation: Lisboa's claim is that the ovens had a social role in sharing news and settling disputes, and choice A gives evidence of both. Choice B supports only the fuel savings she already grants, and D describes the schedule without showing what happened while families waited.

questions.passage: Many wildflowers on the floors of temperate forests, such as trout lilies, do most of their growing in early spring, before the trees overhead leaf out. Once the canopy closes, the forest floor receives only a small fraction of the sunlight that reaches it in early spring. Botanist Anselm Reyes observed that in a year when the trees in one forest leafed out unusually early, spring wildflowers there produced fewer seeds than usual. This observation suggests that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: spring wildflowers produce more seeds in years when trees drop their leaves late in autumn.
the trees in the forest were harmed by competition with the wildflowers.
trout lilies can grow only in forests where the canopy stays closed all year.
the wildflowers depend on the strong sunlight before the canopy closes to gather the energy they need to reproduce.
questions.explanation: An early canopy shortened the sunny period, and seed production fell, so the flowers must rely on that early light. Choice A shifts to autumn, which the observation does not address; C contradicts the text, since the flowers grow while the canopy is open.

questions.passage: Before screw threads were standardized, each machine shop cut screws and nuts to its own specifications, so a bolt made in one shop rarely fit a nut made in another. Historian Imre Kovács notes that as a few common thread standards spread in the nineteenth century, machine owners increasingly ordered replacement parts from distant suppliers rather than having them made by local mechanics. Kovács's observation suggests that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: before thread standards spread, machine owners had no way to replace a broken bolt or nut.
the spread of thread standards reduced machine owners' dependence on nearby workshops that could fit parts to a particular machine.
distant suppliers began cutting screws to the individual specifications of each customer's machine.
local mechanics were the first to propose common thread standards.
questions.explanation: Once threads matched across makers, a part from anywhere would fit, so owners no longer needed a local mechanic to make one to measure. Choice A overstates: owners could still have parts made locally. C contradicts the idea of standard parts, and D is not supported.

questions.passage: Terrace farming turns steep hillsides into a series of flat steps. The level surfaces slow the flow of rainwater down the ______ more water soaks into the soil, and less of it carries topsoil away.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The blank falls between two independent clauses, so a semicolon is needed. A comma alone (A) creates a comma splice, no punctuation (B) creates a run-on, and 'which' (D) produces an ungrammatical clause.

questions.passage: When the travelers finally reached the mountain ______ they discovered that the only inn had closed for the season and that the next bus would not arrive until the following morning.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: 'When the travelers finally reached the mountain village' is a dependent clause, so a comma joins it to the main clause. A semicolon (B) or period (C) would leave the dependent clause standing alone, and a colon (D) must follow an independent clause.

questions.passage: Engineer Hye-jin Park, who has spent a decade designing irrigation systems for small ______ argues that the most useful machines are often the ones that farmers can repair themselves.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The 'who...' clause is a nonessential element that opens with a comma after 'Park,' so a second comma must close it before the main verb 'argues.' A semicolon (A) cannot interrupt a clause, 'and' (B) leaves 'argues' without a subject, and no punctuation (C) leaves the element unclosed.

questions.passage: The dish known in the village simply as 'the Sunday pot'—a slow-cooked mixture of beans, smoked meat, and whatever vegetables the week has ______ is traditionally set on the embers on Saturday night and left untouched until the next afternoon.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The description of the dish is a supplementary element that opens with a dash, so it must close with a matching dash before the main verb 'is.' A comma (A) mismatches the opening dash, a semicolon (C) cannot separate a subject from its verb, and no punctuation (D) leaves the element unclosed.

questions.passage: The roots of a mature oak tree often ______ well beyond the edge of its crown, drawing water from soil far from the trunk, a pattern that gardeners should keep in mind before digging near large trees.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The subject is the plural noun 'roots,' so the verb must be plural: 'extend.' The singular choices agree with 'tree,' which is part of a prepositional phrase and does not govern the verb.

questions.passage: The stone-lined irrigation canal dug by hand in the 1920s still carries water across the whole valley today, although ______ banks have been rebuilt several times after severe floods.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: The banks belong to the canal, a singular noun, so the singular possessive 'its' is needed. 'It's' (C) means 'it is,' 'they're' (B) means 'they are,' and 'their' (A) is plural, with no plural noun for it to refer to.

questions.passage: Since its founding, the town's seed library ______ more than four thousand packets of vegetable seeds to local gardeners, who return a portion of their harvested seed each fall so that the collection can keep growing.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation: 'Since its founding' describes an action that began in the past and continues to the present, which calls for the present perfect 'has lent.' The simple present (B) and future (C) do not fit 'since,' and 'lending' (D) leaves the sentence without a main verb.

questions.passage: Apple trees grown from seed rarely produce fruit like that of the parent tree: a seed from a sweet apple may grow into a tree bearing small, sour fruit. ______ orchard growers propagate favored varieties by grafting, attaching a cutting from the desired tree onto the rootstock of another.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: Because seeds do not reliably reproduce a variety, growers graft instead; the second sentence is a consequence of the first, which 'for this reason' signals. 'For example' (A) would wrongly present grafting as an instance of seeds failing to reproduce their parent's fruit.

questions.passage: Many people assume that the earliest farmers domesticated wheat deliberately, choosing plants with desirable traits. Archaeobotanist Ines Maalouf argues that the process was largely unintentional. ______ harvesters cutting ripe stalks tended to gather plants whose seeds stayed attached rather than scattering, and when some of those seeds were sown the next year, the non-scattering trait gradually became common.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.explanation: The final sentence spells out how Maalouf's unintentional process worked, so 'specifically' fits. 'Instead' (A) is tempting because of the contrast with deliberate selection, but that contrast is already made; placed here, 'instead' would wrongly oppose the final sentence to Maalouf's own claim.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Engineer Amara Diallo designed a pedal-powered water pump for small farms.
• A person operates the pump by stepping on two pedals, as on a stair-climbing machine.
• The pump can lift water from wells up to 7 meters deep.
• It costs about one-tenth as much as a small diesel pump.
questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize how inexpensive Diallo's pump is compared with an alternative. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Diallo's pedal-powered pump can lift water from wells up to 7 meters deep.
A person operates Diallo's pump by stepping on two pedals, as on a stair-climbing machine.
Engineer Amara Diallo designed a pedal-powered water pump for small farms.
Diallo's pedal-powered pump costs about one-tenth as much as a small diesel pump.
questions.explanation: Only choice D gives the pump's cost and compares it with an alternative, a diesel pump. A describes its capacity, B its operation, and C its purpose.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Anthropologist Wen Hollis studied a harvest festival in a farming village in a river valley.
• At the festival, each household brings one dish made from that year's first rice harvest.
• The dishes are set on a single long table, and anyone may eat from any dish.
• Hollis found that households that had quarreled during the year often exchanged dishes directly at the festival.
• She concluded that the shared meal helps repair relationships in the village.
questions.stem: The student wants to present Hollis's conclusion along with the evidence that supports it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Having found that households that had quarreled during the year often exchanged dishes at the festival, Hollis concluded that the shared meal helps repair relationships in the village.
Hollis concluded that the festival's shared meal helps repair relationships in the village.
At the harvest festival Hollis studied, each household brings a dish made from the first rice harvest, and anyone may eat from any dish.
Households that had quarreled during the year often exchanged dishes directly at the festival.
questions.explanation: Choice A pairs the finding about quarreling households with the conclusion drawn from it. B gives the conclusion without evidence, D gives the evidence without the conclusion, and C only describes the festival.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Annual plants, such as sunflowers, grow from seed, flower, and die in a single growing season.
• Perennial plants, such as many grasses, live for several years, regrowing from their roots each spring.
• Most major grain crops, including wheat and rice, are grown as annuals.
• Researchers at the Linwood Agricultural Station are breeding perennial grain crops.
• The deep roots of perennial crops hold soil in place year-round, reducing erosion.
questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize how the crops being bred at the Linwood station differ from most current grain crops. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Perennial plants, such as many grasses, live for several years and regrow from their roots each spring.
The perennial grain crops being bred at the Linwood station have deep roots that hold soil in place year-round.
Whereas most major grain crops, such as wheat and rice, are annuals that die after a single season, the crops being bred at the Linwood station are perennials that regrow for several years.
Unlike sunflowers, which die after a single growing season, many grasses live for several years.
questions.explanation: The goal calls for a contrast between the Linwood crops and most current grains, which choice C makes directly. Choice D draws a contrast, but between sunflowers and grasses, not between the Linwood crops and today's grains; B gives an advantage without the comparison.

questions.passage: Physics teacher Anneliese Varga designed her classroom demonstration to ______ a common intuition. By dropping a coin and a feather inside a long tube from which the air had been pumped out, and showing that the two objects reached the bottom at the same moment, she convinced her students that heavier objects do not naturally fall faster than lighter ones.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: The demonstration shows the intuition that heavier objects fall faster is wrong, so it was meant to dispel it. 'Illustrate' and 'reinforce' would mean the demonstration supported the intuition, the opposite of what happened.

questions.passage: Before voting on the new zoning plan, the Linwood town council held three public hearings and invited written comments from any resident who wished to submit them. Many residents disagreed with the council's final decision, but few could claim that the process leading up to it had been ______.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Hearings and open invitations to comment gave every resident a chance to take part, so few could call the process exclusionary. 'Transparent' and 'deliberate' name qualities the hearings would support, so 'few could claim' makes no sense with them, and three hearings do not rule out a 'prolonged' process.

questions.passage: An understudy may be called on to replace a lead actor with only a few hours' notice, so understudies cannot afford a ______ approach to rehearsal: they learn every line, entrance, and cue of the role, even though they may never perform it in front of an audience.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Because understudies must be fully ready, they cannot take a careless, haphazard approach; the colon describes their thoroughness. 'Meticulous' is the opposite: it describes the approach they do take, so they could certainly 'afford' it.

questions.passage: Playwright Maren Oyelaran's stage directions are notably ______. Where most scripts describe a set in careful detail, hers often consist of a single line, such as 'A kitchen. Morning.' Directors and designers must supply everything else themselves.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.explanation: Directions of a single line that leave everything else to directors are spare, or minimal. 'Cryptic' is tempting, but 'A kitchen. Morning.' is brief rather than puzzling, and 'precise' contradicts the contrast with detailed scripts.

questions.passage: Hailstones can grow as large as golf balls, yet they often fall during storms on hot summer afternoons. The explanation lies in the structure of the storm clouds that produce them. Powerful updrafts inside these clouds carry water droplets thousands of meters upward, where temperatures are far below freezing. There, a small ice pellet collides with droplets that freeze onto its surface, adding layer after layer of ice until the stone becomes too heavy for the updraft to hold up and falls to the ground.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It describes a common belief about hail and then explains why that belief is mistaken.
It compares hail with other forms of frozen precipitation.
It explains how hail damages crops and then describes ways to limit that damage.
It presents a seemingly puzzling fact and then explains how it comes about.
questions.explanation: The text opens with a puzzle (large balls of ice on hot afternoons) and then explains the updrafts and freezing that produce them. No mistaken belief is described, so choice A misreads the opening, and the text never discusses other precipitation or crop damage.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a story. Wen, a young dancer, is watching her teacher demonstrate a turn.

Madame Serrano did not explain the turn. She simply performed it, once at half speed and once at full speed, and then stood waiting with her hands folded. Wen had expected instructions: where to place her weight, when to whip her head around. Instead there was only the memory of the teacher's body in motion, already fading. Wen understood, with some alarm, that she was being asked to learn the way Madame Serrano herself must once have learned: by watching until watching was no longer enough.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the final sentence?
choices: It reveals Wen's recognition of what her teacher's wordless demonstration requires of her.
It suggests that Madame Serrano performed the turn poorly on purpose.
It explains why Wen had expected her teacher to give detailed instructions.
It conveys Wen's frustration that her teacher is unwilling to share what she knows.
questions.explanation: The final sentence shows Wen grasping that she must learn by watching and then trying, as her teacher once did. Her 'alarm' is anxiety about the task, not resentment, and the teacher is sharing her knowledge by demonstrating, so choice D misreads the sentence.

questions.passage: In participatory budgeting, residents rather than officials propose and vote on how to spend part of a city's budget. Supporters usually measure such programs by what gets built: playgrounds repaired, crosswalks painted, streetlights installed. Political scientist Marisol Etxeberria argues that this focus overlooks the programs' more lasting effect. In the cities she studied, residents who had voted in participatory budgeting were more likely than their neighbors to attend other public meetings years later, long after the projects they had chosen were finished.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe the process by which residents propose and select projects in participatory budgeting.
To introduce a perspective that shifts attention from one outcome of participatory budgeting to another that its supporters tend to overlook.
To question whether the projects funded through participatory budgeting actually benefit residents.
To compare participatory budgeting with the traditional way cities set their budgets.
questions.explanation: The text moves from the usual measure (what gets built) to Etxeberria's point that the programs' more lasting effect is on residents' later civic participation. Choice C is tempting, but the text never doubts that the projects help; it says only that focusing on them misses something.

questions.passage:
Text 1
Meteorologist Dagny Holm points out that weather forecasts have improved steadily for decades: a five-day forecast today is about as accurate as a three-day forecast was a generation ago. Holm credits these gains mainly to faster computers running more detailed models, and she predicts that with enough computing power, forecasters will someday be able to say whether it will rain in a particular town on a particular day a month in advance.

Text 2
The atmosphere is a chaotic system: small errors in measurements of its present state grow larger as a forecast runs forward in time. Because the atmosphere can never be measured perfectly, forecasts of day-to-day weather lose their value after about two weeks, however detailed the model. Longer-range forecasts can still indicate whether a coming month is likely to be wetter or warmer than usual.
questions.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Holm's prediction?
choices: By agreeing that faster computers will eventually make it possible to forecast daily weather a month in advance.
By disputing Holm's claim that forecasts have become more accurate over the past several decades.
By contending that the limit on forecasting specific daily weather far ahead comes from the impossibility of measuring the atmosphere perfectly, not from a lack of computing power.
By claiming that forecasts extending beyond two weeks provide no useful information at all.
questions.explanation: Text 2 says daily forecasts lose value after about two weeks 'however detailed the model' because measurement errors grow, which rejects Holm's reliance on computing power. Choice D overstates Text 2, whose final sentence says longer-range forecasts can still be useful for general tendencies.

questions.passage: Dance notation systems, which record movement with symbols on a page, have existed for centuries, but relatively few dancers or choreographers have learned to use them. Instead, most dances have been passed from one generation to the next much as folk songs once were: dancers who performed a work taught it directly to younger dancers. Dance historian Yusuf Adeyemi points out a consequence of this practice. Because each teacher remembered the steps slightly differently, a ballet performed today may differ in many small ways from the version first staged, even when the company believes it is presenting the original.
questions.stem: According to the text, why might a ballet performed today differ from the version first staged?
choices: Choreographers today often change older dances to suit modern audiences.
Dance notation systems lack symbols for many kinds of movement.
Most ballet companies today have fewer dancers than companies did in the past.
Teachers who passed the dance down remembered its steps in slightly different ways.
questions.explanation: The text says each teacher 'remembered the steps slightly differently,' so small changes built up. Choice B misreads the point about notation: the problem is that few people learned to use it, not that it lacks symbols.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a story. Mr. Halloran is the superintendent of an apartment building.

Tenants complained about the radiators every winter, and every winter Mr. Halloran climbed the stairs with his wrench and his patience. He knew each radiator by its noise: the one in 3B that knocked twice and stopped, the one in 5A that hissed like a kettle. When the owners announced that a new heating system would be installed in the spring, the tenants cheered. Mr. Halloran said it was good news. Then he went down to the basement and sat for a long while beside the old boiler, listening to it tick as it cooled.
questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Although Mr. Halloran says he welcomes the new heating system, he privately feels a sense of loss at the thought of the old one being replaced.
Mr. Halloran doubts that the new heating system will work any better than the old one.
The tenants are ungrateful for the years Mr. Halloran spent repairing the radiators.
Mr. Halloran is relieved that he will no longer have to answer the tenants' complaints.
questions.explanation: Mr. Halloran calls the news good, yet he knows each radiator intimately and sits quietly beside the old boiler, suggesting attachment and loss. Choice D is tempting, but his lingering beside the boiler shows reluctance, not relief, and nothing suggests he doubts the new system (B).

questions.passage: Meteorologist Kwame Ansah-Boateng hypothesizes that nighttime temperatures in Ferrow City stay higher than those in the surrounding countryside because the city's pavement and stone buildings absorb heat from the sun during the day and release it slowly after sunset.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ansah-Boateng's hypothesis?
choices: Daytime high temperatures in Ferrow City and the surrounding countryside are nearly identical in summer.
On clear nights, Ferrow City's paved downtown is consistently several degrees warmer than nearby farmland, and the difference grows in the hours after sunset.
Ferrow City receives slightly more rain each year than the surrounding countryside.
A large, grassy park in Ferrow City is cooler during the day than the paved streets around it.
questions.explanation: The hypothesis concerns nighttime warmth from heat released slowly after sunset; choice B shows the paved city staying warmer than farmland, with the gap widening after dark. Choice D involves pavement but reports daytime temperatures, which the hypothesis does not address.

questions.passage:
Turnout in Municipal Elections Before and After a Change in Election Date

Town       Before change  After change
Halvern    18%            47%
Mossbury   22%            51%
Quillon    25%            29%
Tarrow     15%            44%

Four towns moved their municipal elections from a separate spring date to the November date on which statewide elections are held. A political scientist claims that the change was followed by a large increase in turnout in most of the towns but by only a small increase in one of them. She supports the claim by noting that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: turnout in Halvern rose from 18% to 47% after the change.
Tarrow had the lowest turnout of the four towns before the change.
turnout rose by 29 percentage points in Halvern, Mossbury, and Tarrow but by only 4 points in Quillon.
Mossbury had the highest turnout of the four towns after the change.
questions.explanation: The claim contrasts large gains in most towns with a small gain in one, and only choice C gives both. Choice A describes one large increase but leaves out the exception.

questions.passage: Theater researcher Beatriz Kowalczyk hypothesizes that audiences laugh more at a comedy when a theater is full than when it is nearly empty, and not simply because a full theater contains more people. In her view, each individual audience member laughs more often when surrounded by others who are laughing.
questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Kowalczyk's hypothesis?
